scenes.title: Talavera
scenes.subject: Inside a traditional Talavera workshop in Puebla, Mexico, medium shot: a smiling Mexican woman artisan in a checked cotton apron sits at a wooden table and hand-paints a medium round plate lying flat on a small grey banding wheel, the whole plate clearly visible in the centre. The plate is coated in raw, unfired tin glaze: chalky, matte, milky white with no shine. With a long, thin handmade brush of fine dark hair on a wooden stick she paints a bold cobalt flower in the middle; the fresh pigment looks soft and dusty blue, and the rest of the pattern is only a faint grey charcoal outline. Her other fingertips rest on the rim. Small ceramic cups of thick blue, yellow and black pigment stand beside the plate. Behind her, plank shelves hold rows of matte white unpainted pieces and a few finished glossy cobalt-and-yellow Talavera jars. Worn plaster walls, warm window light.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. The artisan lifts the brush from the flower, dips it into the cup of cobalt pigment, and rests the loaded tip still on the outer rim of the plate. With her other hand she slowly spins the banding wheel: as the plate turns under the motionless brush, a continuous thick cobalt-blue line appears exactly where the bristles touch the rim and stays, growing around the plate until it closes into a full blue ring. The plate's painted flower turns with the plate and stays unchanged. One person, natural hands; she looks up and smiles.

scenes.title: Barro Negro
scenes.subject: A barro negro pottery workshop in San Bartolo Coyotepec, Oaxaca, medium shot: an older Zapotec woman artisan with grey braids, a plain white cotton blouse and a checked apron sits on a low wooden stool and burnishes a round, nearly dry, unfired clay jar (cántaro). The jar stands on a woven palm ring on a low wooden table in front of her, fully visible in the centre of the frame. Its surface is earthy brownish-grey and matte, with one freshly polished band that has a soft satin sheen. Between her fingertips she rubs a small smooth white quartz pebble over the clay while her other hand rests on the jar. Beside it, a clay bowl of water. On plain wooden shelves behind her stand finished barro negro pieces: unglazed charcoal-black jars with a soft metallic pewter sheen, some with carved openwork, on woven rings. Ochre plaster walls, warm daylight.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. The artisan moves the white quartz pebble from the jar's mouth down onto the dull grey-brown shoulder just above the dark polished band. Holding it flat under her thumb and fingertips, she rubs with firm pressure in short, overlapping back-and-forth strokes, working slowly sideways along the band's upper edge. Wherever the pebble passes, the matte clay is pressed smooth and turns darker with a soft satin shine, so the polished band visibly grows upward and the new shine stays; clay she has not rubbed stays matte. Her left hand stays on the jar's side, holding it steady. The jar keeps its shape and place on the palm rings, never turned or lifted. Near the end she smiles.

scenes.title: Árbol de la Vida
scenes.subject: A family pottery workshop in Metepec, State of Mexico, medium shot: a smiling middle-aged Mexican artisan man in a paint-flecked work shirt sits at a wooden table and paints an Árbol de la Vida clay sculpture standing in front of him, fully visible in the centre with space above it. The tree is a symmetrical candelabra shape on a bell-shaped base, with curving arched branches, small Adam and Eve figures dressed in leaves on either side of the trunk, a serpent coiled around it and a sun face at the top, all covered with flat stylised clay flowers, leaves and little birds. The upper half is already painted in fresh, opaque Mexican pink, yellow, turquoise, green and red with fine black outlines; the lower branches are still bare orange fired terracotta. With a fine brush he paints one flower pink. Small paint jars on the table; shelves of unpainted terracotta pieces behind. Warm light.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. The artisan dips his fine brush into the open jar of pink paint at the front of the table, then brings it to the large bare orange terracotta flower on the lower left branch, just below his hand. He lays the loaded brush on one petal and draws it from the flower's centre out to the petal tip, then paints the next petal, and the next: opaque pink covers the orange clay exactly where the bristles pass and stays, so petal by petal the flower turns pink while its centre stays bare clay. The tree of life stands still and keeps its shape and all its other colours; only the brush touches it. He glances up and smiles. One person only.

scenes.title: Alebrijes
scenes.subject: Photorealistic medium shot on the shaded patio workshop of a family home in San Martín Tilcajete, Oaxaca. A smiling Zapotec woman with a long braid sits at a sturdy wooden table covered in paint-stained paper, painting a hand-carved copal-wood alebrije: a winged jaguar about 40 cm long standing on four legs in the centre of the table, fully visible, with separately carved ears, wings and curled tail. Its head, wings and front half are already painted a smooth solid cobalt blue, the head decorated with fine yellow, orange and white lines and Zapotec step-frets; but its hindquarters, back legs and tail are still BARE PALE CREAM CARVED WOOD with visible knife facets, not painted yet. She holds a medium brush loaded with cobalt-blue paint against the bare wood where the blue ends. An open plastic pot of cobalt-blue paint stands right beside the alebrije. Around it: other small paint pots, a cup of water, a pale unpainted copal figure. Background: turquoise wall, shelf of finished alebrijes. Warm afternoon light, no text or labels.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. She dips the brush into the open pot of cobalt-blue paint beside the alebrije, then lays it on the bare pale wood of the jaguar's hindquarters right where the blue ends and pulls smooth strokes along the carved surface: opaque cobalt blue covers the pale wood exactly where the bristles pass and stays, stroke after stroke, so the blue area steadily grows back over the hip and down the back leg. She reloads the brush once. The alebrije stands still on the table, keeps its shape and the finished patterns on its head, and is never lifted or turned. One person, natural hands; near the end she looks up and smiles.

scenes.title: Tapetes Zapotecos
scenes.subject: Photorealistic medium shot of a family weaving workshop in Teotitlán del Valle, Oaxaca. A smiling middle-aged Zapotec man in a plain checked shirt sits at the front of a large handmade treadle loom: a heavy box frame of thick square pine timbers. Taut white cotton warp threads run horizontally away from him at waist height and pass through the comb-like reed of the loom's heavy hanging wooden beater frame, which swings from the overhead frame on two side arms; both his hands grip the plain, unmarked top bar of that frame just in front of him. Below the beater, lying flat on the loom over the front beam, is the half-woven wool rug: a dense flat tapestry weave with a stepped diamond and a Mitla step-fret border in cochineal red, indigo blue, pericón gold, natural cream and undyed brown; the rows being woven now, at the top edge of the rug against the warp, form a wide band of cochineal red. A long wooden boat shuttle wound with red wool rests on the woven edge. Behind him, whitewashed walls hung with finished rugs and skeins of naturally dyed yarn. Warm daylight, no text. Every wooden part is plain and unmarked, with no letters or words anywhere.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. The weaver pushes the hanging beater away from him, picks up the wooden shuttle and throws it through the open gap in the white warp from right to left, unreeling one strand of red wool across the full width, then grabs the beater with both hands and pulls it firmly toward him, packing the new red row against the woven edge. He repeats this twice; each pass adds one more thin red row, so the red band at the top of the rug grows a little toward the beater and stays. The rug's pattern and the loom stay unchanged. One person, natural hands; he looks up and smiles.

scenes.title: Arte Huichol
scenes.subject: Photorealistic medium close-up of a Wixárika (Huichol) artisan at work in a simple adobe-walled home in the Sierra of northern Jalisco. A smiling young Wixárika woman in a bright emerald-green puffed-sleeve blouse with red ribbon trim, a purple paisley bandana and a wide netted bead collar sits at a wooden table; her hands and a carved wooden jaguar head about 25 cm long fill the lower half of the frame, close to the camera. The jaguar's snout, open mouth with white beaded fangs and eyes are covered in tight neat rows of tiny glass seed beads in turquoise, cobalt, red, white and black; its whole forehead is still a large smooth area of bare amber beeswax, and along the edge of the beadwork one short row of bright yellow beads has been started. With a fine needle in her right hand, threaded with several yellow beads, she touches the wax at the end of that yellow row; her left fingertips steady the jaguar's ear. A small dish of yellow beads sits beside it. Warm window light, no text.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. With the fine needle she slides the yellow beads off one at a time onto the bare amber wax at the end of the started row, nudging each one in with the needle point so it sits snugly against the last; each bead stays exactly where it is set, so the bright yellow row visibly grows along the edge of the beadwork across the forehead. She dips the needle into the dish to pick up more yellow beads and continues. Her left fingertips stay on the ear; the jaguar head never moves or changes shape. One person, natural hands; she glances up and smiles.

scenes.title: Papel Picado
scenes.subject: Photorealistic medium shot of a family papel picado workshop in San Salvador Huixcolotla, Puebla, Mexico. A smiling Mexican artisan in a plain cotton shirt sits at a worn wooden table, centred in frame, leaning over his work. On the table lies a flat, dull grey lead plate, and on it a neat, squared block of about fifty sheets of thin tissue paper whose edges show pink, orange, purple and lime-green layers, topped by a pale paper pattern with a black-line drawing of flowers and a dove under clear plastic. His LEFT HAND GRIPS a slim pen-sized steel chisel upright in his fist, its small flat blade tip resting on a drawn black line of a flower petal; his RIGHT HAND holds a small round-faced hammer with a short wooden handle, raised a few centimetres above the top of the chisel, about to tap it. A few petal shapes are already cut out of the pattern showing the coloured layers beneath, and tiny coloured paper plugs lie beside the stack. Rows of thin steel chisels with different tips lie beside the plate. Behind him hang strings of finished papel picado flags. Warm workshop light, no text or signs.
scenes.motion: His left hand holds the thin steel chisel upright in his fist, its tip on the black line of a flower petal. His right hand lifts the small hammer a few centimetres and strikes the top of the chisel in quick, light taps; with each tap the chisel edge sinks deeper into the paper stack. He lifts the chisel, sets it a few millimetres further along the petal outline and taps again, until the outline is cut all round; then he pries the cut piece out with the chisel tip, leaving a clean petal-shaped hole, and the small multicoloured paper plug drops beside the stack. The stack, drawing and lead plate never move and nothing else changes. One person, natural hands; he glances up and smiles.

scenes.title: Piñatas
scenes.subject: Photorealistic medium shot of a family piñata workshop in Acolman, State of Mexico. A smiling Mexican woman artisan in a simple apron stands behind a wooden worktable, centred in frame. On the table, with space all around it, sits a traditional seven-point star piñata about eighty centimetres across, resting steady on its lower cones: a round central body covered in shiny gold metallic paper and seven cardboard cones radiating in all directions, each covered in glossy pink, blue or silver foil, with rings of finely fringed tissue paper in purple, turquoise, yellow and green around the base and long tissue streamers at the tips. Her fingertips press a fringed pink tissue band around one cone. Scissors, a stack of tissue paper sheets and a bowl of flour paste with a brush lie on the table. Behind her, unpainted terracotta clay pots are stacked and finished star piñatas hang from wooden beams. Warm light, no text or signs.
scenes.motion: Her right hand carries the loose end of a long, narrow strip of pink fringed tissue once around the silver cone, just above the pink rows already there, and her thumb presses the strip's plain, paste-wet upper edge onto the silver foil every few centimetres. Wherever she presses, the strip sticks flat and stays, so a new ring of pink fringe forms above the old ones, its cut strands hanging loose over the row below like roof tiles. Her left hand steadies the star. The star keeps its shape, colours and position and is never lifted or turned; the hanging piñatas stay still. One person, natural hands; she looks up and smiles.

scenes.title: Cartonería
scenes.subject: Photorealistic medium shot of a family cartonería workshop of the Linares tradition in Merced Balbuena, Mexico City. A smiling Mexican artisan in his fifties, with glasses, a grey sweater vest and paint-splattered trousers, sits at a wooden workbench crusted with dried paste and paint drips, centred in frame. On the bench, fully visible, stands a papier-mâché alebrije about half a metre long: a winged dragon with small horns, a spiky green crest, bulging yellow eyes, white fangs and a curled tail. Its head, body and left wing are already painted glossy red, yellow, cobalt blue and green with black outlines, but its large RIGHT WING, facing the camera, is still plain matte WHITE PRIMER over the paper, with no colour yet; a narrow strip near the wing's base is already painted bright red. He holds a medium flat brush loaded with red paint against the white wing. An open jar of red paint stands right beside the wing. Around him: a plastic bowl of white flour paste, newspapers, a roll of brown kraft paper, an unpainted kraft-paper skeleton, a white Catrina skull under a blue hat and a red horned Judas devil. Warm light, no text or signs.
scenes.motion: Start from this exact frame. The artisan dips the flat brush into the open jar of red paint beside the wing, then lays it on the white primer of the dragon's right wing next to the red strip and pulls long, smooth strokes outward along the wing: opaque glossy red covers the white exactly where the bristles pass and stays, stroke after stroke, so the red area steadily grows across the wing until about half of it is red. He reloads the brush once. His other hand rests on the bench. The dragon keeps its shape, position and all its other colours and is never lifted or turned. One person, natural hands; near the end he looks up and smiles.

scenes.title: Plata de Taxco
scenes.subject: A small family silversmith workshop in Taxco, Guerrero, medium shot: a smiling Mexican silversmith in a striped long-sleeved shirt sits at a worn wooden workbench against a whitewashed wall hung with pliers, scissors and small saws. In the centre of the bench, fully visible, a wide sterling-silver cuff bracelet with a freshly hammered, sparkling texture rests on a tapered steel bracelet mandrel held horizontally in a small bench vise. He taps the cuff with a small polished jeweller's hammer, his other hand resting on the bench. Around him: a hand-cranked steel rolling mill bolted to the bench, a brass soldering torch with a rubber hose lying on two firebricks, a magnifying visor pushed up on his forehead, and a few finished pieces on a cloth: mirror-bright silver earrings and a pendant inlaid with black obsidian and green malachite. A small window shows white houses with red tile roofs on a steep green hill. Warm afternoon light.
scenes.motion: The silversmith's left hand moves from the bench to the cuff and holds its side against the mandrel with his fingertips, clear of the hammer. With the small polished hammer he taps the top of the cuff, where the silver rests on the steel mandrel, in quick, light, even blows; each tap lands flat on the silver and leaves a small, fresh, mirror-bright facet, the taps stepping across the width of the band so a new row of bright facets forms. After the row he turns the cuff slightly on the mandrel and starts the next row. The cuff keeps its round shape and width; the mandrel and vise never move; the hammer never hits bare steel. One person, natural hands; he glances up and smiles.

scenes.title: Cobre Martillado
scenes.subject: A traditional coppersmith workshop in Santa Clara del Cobre, Michoacán, medium shot: one smiling Purépecha coppersmith in a plain grey T-shirt, jeans, a cap and a worn suede apron stands beside a waist-high tree stump with a long curved steel stake (bordón) set into it, the stake's end pointing toward him. A half-formed round copper vase LIES ON ITS SIDE with its open mouth slid over the end of the stake, so the stake is inside the vase; its surface is covered in small overlapping hammer facets, matte salmon-pink patched with smoky blue-violet fire colours, not glowing. His left hand grips the vase's rim with long iron tongs; his right hand raises a short heavy hammer with a worn wooden handle above the vase's belly, directly over the end of the stake inside it. Behind him, softly out of focus: soot-darkened adobe-brick walls under an open shed roof, a low wood fire on the earth floor, stacked pine firewood, and a rough shelf with a polished hammered-copper pitcher. Warm firelight mixed with soft daylight.
scenes.motion: The coppersmith brings the short, heavy hammer down onto the upper side of the copper vase's belly, directly over the end of the steel stake inside it, in a slow, steady rhythm; the copper is hot from the fire but not glowing. Each blow lands squarely on the copper and leaves one small new flat facet, slightly brighter, right beside the previous one. After every two blows his left hand slowly turns the vase a few centimetres on the stake with the tongs, so the next blow meets fresh metal and a short row of new facets forms around the belly. The vase keeps its round shape, size, colours and place on the stake, with no sparks, dents or cracks. The fire flickers behind him; one person, natural hands; between blows he smiles.

scenes.title: Vidrio Soplado
scenes.subject: A traditional blown-glass workshop (vidriera) in Tlaquepaque, Jalisco, medium shot: a young Mexican glassblower in a plain grey T-shirt, jeans and a cap stands with his LIPS SEALED AROUND THE MOUTHPIECE of a long steel blowpipe, cheeks gently puffed as he blows, his eyes looking at the glass; one hand near his mouth steadies the pipe and the other hand further down rolls it. The pipe angles down diagonally toward the viewer and at its lower end, near the centre of the frame and fully visible, glows a small orange-hot bubble of molten glass the size of a grapefruit, round and centred on the pipe. Behind him, softly out of focus: a squat brick furnace clad in sooty steel sheets with a small rectangular opening glowing yellow-white, a flat steel table, a concrete floor, and a wooden shelf of finished Jalisco glass: thick hand-blown tumblers and round jugs with tiny bubbles and cobalt-blue rims, and spheres in ruby red, emerald green and amber. Warm orange furnace light.
scenes.motion: The glassblower closes his lips around the end of the blowpipe and blows two long, gentle breaths, cheeks filling and relaxing, while his lower hand keeps rolling the pipe slowly and continuously on its own long axis, like a rolling pin, never stopping. With each breath the glowing glass bubble at the end swells a little, staying round, centred and attached, until it is about a third larger; its glow slowly deepens from bright orange to a darker orange as it cools. The pipe keeps the same angle and place and does not swing; the glass never drips, sags or detaches. The furnace glows behind him; one person, natural hands; between breaths his eyes smile.
